Data Imbalance - Health Insurance¶

By: Francisco da Ana (up202108762)

For this assignement related to Imbalaced Data, I will be using the Health Insurance dataset already explored in the first and second assignements (Data Profiling & Data Complexity).

From the suggested tasks for this assignement, I chose project B:

"Perform a case study on imbalanced learning ... You can start by profiling your data and decide on which

performance metric(s) to optimize ... Then, select a few classification methods ... Finally, apply different techniques for addressing the class imbalance issue"

First, let's remember the dataset characteristics and the main objective of the dataset:

It contains 15 attributes (1 target and 14 features) and 72458 instances. The target variable is health_ins, which is a binary feature that indicates if the individual has health insurance or not. The dataset contains both numerical and categorical features.

The attributes are:

  • unnamed | numeric: an index column
  • custid | text: the unique ID of the customer
  • sex | categorical: the gender of the customer
  • is_employed | boolean: indicates whether the customer is employed or not
  • income | numeric: numerical value representing the customer's income
  • marital_status | categorical: the marital status of the customer
  • health_ins | boolean: indicates whether the customer has health insurance or not. This can be the target variable in the context of a classification problem.
  • housing_type | categorical: describes the situation of the customer's habitation
  • num_vehicles | numeric: the number of vehicles the customer owns
  • age | numeric: the age of the customer in years
  • state_of_res | text: the US state where the customer resides
  • code_column | numeric: likely a categorical or code-based feature (potentially related to location or demographics).
  • gas_usage | numeric: a measure of the customer's gas usage
  • rooms | numeric: the number of rooms in the customer's house
  • recent_move_b | boolean: indicator if the customer has recently moved

Remembering the previous analysis¶

Our target variable is highly imbalanced, with a IR of around 10. Data complexity measure "Entropy of class proportions" is 0.561. A value like this for a binary classification problem indicates a considerable level of class imbalance that may require techniques to address the imbalance and ensure the model's performance is robust across both classes.

Performance of some classifiers¶

Before treating the imbalance issue, let's apply 2 simple classifiers to the dataset and check their performance metrics. We will use the following classifiers:

  • Decision Tree
  • K-Nearest Neighbors
In [341]:
target = 'health_ins'
X = df.drop(target, axis=1)
y = df[target]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, shuffle=True)

For this dataset, in the previous assignement we verified the best F1 score is achieved for the following hyperparameters:

  • Decision Tree: max_depth=5
  • K-Nearest Neighbors: n_neighbors=20

Decision Tree¶

In [342]:
imb_dt_max5 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=42)
imb_dt_max5.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = imb_dt_max5.predict(X_test)
print(f'Accuracy: {round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),4)} | F1: {round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred),4)}')

Accuracy: 0.9096 | F1: 0.9527

This seems very good! Accuracy rounds 91% and F1 95%. But let's see the confusion matrix.

In [343]:
cm_imb_dt_max5 = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm_imb_dt_max5).plot()
tp, tn, fp, fn = cm_imb_dt_max5[1,1], cm_imb_dt_max5[0,0], cm_imb_dt_max5[0,1], cm_imb_dt_max5[1,0]

# Specificity is the proportion of actual negative cases that are correctly identified.
spec = round(tn/(tn+fp),3)*100
print(f'Specificity: {spec}%')

Specificity: 0.0%

The performance metrics are very misleading. The model is absolutely biased towards the majority class, since it basically classifies all cases as positive.

From the whole training partition (≈21k cases), it only classified 4 cases as negative... and it still failed on all of them. The testing process resulted in absolutely 0 True Negatives.

What if we we don't limit the tree's depth? Will the model overfit?

In [344]:
imb_dt_nomax = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)
imb_dt_nomax.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = imb_dt_nomax.predict(X_test)
print(f'Accuracy: {round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),4)} | F1: {round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred),4)}')

Accuracy: 0.8461 | F1: 0.9148

Worse performance...?

In [345]:
cm_imb_dt_nomax = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm_imb_dt_nomax).plot()

tp, tn, fp, fn = cm_imb_dt_nomax[1,1], cm_imb_dt_nomax[0,0], cm_imb_dt_nomax[0,1], cm_imb_dt_nomax[1,0]
spec = round(tn/(tn+fp),3)*100
print(f'Specificity: {spec}%')

Specificity: 22.0%

Even with "worse" metrics, the "overfitted" decision tree is more able of capturiing the minority class. There were 422 true negatives in the testing process, which is a huge improvement on the "optimized" tree, besides the lower accuracy and F1 score.

Specificity increased from absolute 0 to 22%, which is still very low, but it's a start.

In [349]:
cm_imb_knn_k2 = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm_imb_knn_k2).plot()

tp, tn, fp, fn = cm_imb_knn_k2[1,1], cm_imb_knn_k2[0,0], cm_imb_knn_k2[0,1], cm_imb_knn_k2[1,0]
spec = round(tn/(tn+fp),3)*100
print(f'Specificity: {spec}%')

Specificity: 30.8%

KNN classifier shows very ineteresting insights. The more neighbors it considers, the more underfitted the model becomes and the more biased towards the majority class it gets. And, since the training set is very imbalanced, the model will better predict the majority class.

This is the proof that an "overfitted" model may be better for capturing the minority class in an imbalanced dataset.

How do max_depth and k affett specificity of, respectively, Decision Tree and KNN classifiers?

In [350]:
dt_measures = pd.DataFrame(columns=['max_depth', 'specificity'])
parameters = list(range(3, 35)) + [None]

for max_depth in parameters:
    print(f'Fitting model with {max_depth}')
    model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=max_depth, random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
    spec = round(tn/(tn+fp),3)
    new_row = {'max_depth': max_depth, 'specificity': spec}
    dt_measures.loc[len(dt_measures)] = new_row

    if max_depth == None:
        print(f'None generates the following depth: {model.get_depth()}')


sns.lineplot(x='max_depth', y='specificity', data=dt_measures)

Once we divided an imbalanced dataset to both train and validate our models, the "classical" metrics are not enough to reason about model performance.

This dataset is highly imbalanced, meaning that both test and validation partitions (generated from itself) will have a similar distribution. So, if we use a model that learns to predict everything as positive, when tested in a dataset with similar distribution, it will achieve very good accuracy, F1, ... metrics.

These plots show that, increasing tree depth and decreasing number of neighbors will increase specificity, which is a good indicator of how well the model is capturing the minority class.

Dealing with the imbalance issue¶

Resampling Techniques¶

These are methods which, respectively, remove examples of the majority class and generate samples for the minority class in order to balance the dataset. They will be applied to the training set only, to avoid data leakage and keep data integrity.

The classical approach to put this in practice is SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique). This technique generates synthetic samples for any instances of the the minority class by interpolating between existing samples. This is a very popular approach for dealing with imbalanced datasets.

The following SMOTE variants will be applied:

  • SMOTE: the original technique
  • Random Over-sampling: generates synthetic samples by randomly selecting a minority class instance and adding noise to it
  • Borderline-SMOTE: a variant of SMOTE that focuses on the instances that are near the decision boundary
  • ADASYN: a variant of SMOTE that generates synthetic samples based on the density of the minority class instances, focusing on the regions that are more difficult to learn
  • SVM-SMOTE: a variant of SMOTE that uses an SVM classifier to identify the instances that are near the decision boundary and generate synthetic samples for them
  • SMOTE-ENN: combination of over-sampling and under-sampling, which applies SMOTE to the minority class and then removes the samples of majority class that are near the decision boundary
  • SMOTE-TomekLinks: combination of over-sampling and under-sampling, which applies SMOTE to the minority class and then removes the samples that are near the decision boundary

Due to the high computational cost of TSNE visualization, we will compare the characteristics of resampled datasets using some Data Complexity Measures: F1, F2, F3, F4.

In [353]:
def get_data_complexity(X, y):
    return {
        'f1' : round(pbx.f1(X, y),3),
        'f2' : round(pbx.f2(X, y),3),
        'f3' : round(pbx.f3(X, y),3),
        'f4' : round(pbx.f4(X, y),3),
    }

def print_target_dist(y, dataset_name):
    print(f"Frequency in {dataset_name} dataset: {y.value_counts()}")
    print(f"Percentage in {dataset_name} dataset: {y.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3)}")

plt.scatter(fb_measures['dataset'], fb_measures['f2'], color='g', label='F2', marker='x')

plt.legend()
plt.title('F1, F2, F3, F4 measures')
plt.show()

Remembering the meaning of each measure:

  • F1: class separability
  • F2: feature overlap
  • F3: best single feature
  • F4: combined feature effectiveness

The objective is to find a good trade-off between high F1 and low F2.

SVM-SMOTE seems to be the best technique, because even with a lower F1 measure, it has a significant lower F2 measure.

Model (re-)evaluation¶

In [365]:
# Function to, given the prediction of a model, return its performance metrics
def get_metrics(y_pred):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
    acc = round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),3)
    prec = round(precision_score(y_test, y_pred),3)
    rec = round(recall_score(y_test, y_pred),3)
    f1 = round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred),3)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
    spec = round(tn / (tn+fp),3)
    gmean = round(np.sqrt(rec*spec),3)
    return {'accuracy': acc, 'precision': prec, 'recall': rec, 'f1': f1, 'specificity': spec, 'gmean': gmean, 'cm': cm}
In [366]:
def plot_measures(measures):
    parameters = measures.iloc[:,0]
    accuracy = measures.iloc[:,1]
    precision = measures.iloc[:,2]
    recall = measures.iloc[:,3]
    f1 = measures.iloc[:,4]
    spec = measures.iloc[:,5]
    gmean = measures.iloc[:,6]

    sns.lineplot(x=parameters, y=accuracy, label='accuracy')
    sns.lineplot(x=parameters, y=precision, label='precision')
    sns.lineplot(x=parameters, y=recall, label='recall')
    sns.lineplot(x=parameters, y=f1, label='f1')
    sns.lineplot(x=parameters, y=spec, label='specificity')
    sns.lineplot(x=parameters, y=gmean, label='gmean')

def plot_models_perf(results):
    melted = results.melt(id_vars="model", value_vars=["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "specificity"],
                        var_name="measure", value_name="value")

    plt.figure(figsize=(20, 7))
    sns.barplot(data=melted, x="model", y="value", hue="measure", palette="deep")
    plt.title("Model Performance Comparison", fontsize=16)
    plt.xlabel("Model", fontsize=20)
    plt.ylabel("Value", fontsize=20)
    plt.xticks(fontsize=20)
    plt.yticks(fontsize=20)
    plt.legend(title="Measure", fontsize=20, title_fontsize=20)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

After rebalancing techniques, our models became much more capable of capturing negatives cases (minority class). Specificity increased to around 70%. However, the "classical" performance metrics decreased a bit but this was expected, since the validation set does now follow the same distribution as the training set (imbalanced vs balanced).
